name: Dusky Violet
lede: Dusky Violet is a dim, greyed blue-violet, built by putting the modifier dusky in front of the base color violet rather than naming anything in particular.

sections.title: A modifier on violet
sections.body:
Dusky Violet puts the modifier word dusky in front of the base color [[violet]], in the compound-modifier grammar ColorHub's library uses for descriptive names like this one [1]. Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* carries the swatch as plate XXIII, hue 59', an aged plate scan read as approximate [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[yvette-violet]], 3.0 units off [1]; [[dark-bluish-violet]] sits 3.2 off and [[dark-madder-violet]] 3.7 [1], all close enough on screen to blur together in low light.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color within six units of this swatch in 74 of 23,781 paintings, 0.31 percent, as photographed; looking inside each painting for at least five percent coverage narrows that to 42 [2]. That makes it rarer than 52 percent of the named colors in our library [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 0.5 percent of our 1,674 paintings from that decade, 2.2 times the museums' baseline rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often sits as a hidden color, in 60 percent of its 42 appearances by lightness rank [2].

The earliest match, Bartolomeo Vivarini's work, dates to 1490, more than four centuries before the name's 1912 record, so it marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment [2].
